description: OpenAI is running up against the clock. The ChatGPT maker has until the end of the year to complete a complicated transition from a non-profit to a for-profit entity in order to get its hands on a majority of its late March $40 billion funding round–the largest private tech fundraise to date. The restructuring has been challenged by former cofounder-turned-rival Elon Musk, who has asked authorities to block the transition and at one point offered to buy the nonprofit that controls OpenAI. But the $300 billion-valued behemoth continues to grow: 500 million people now use conversational bot ChatGPT weekly and it has some 2 million paying enterprise users. In March, the AI juggernaut added more advanced image generation capabilities to ChatGPT, setting off a viral and controversial trend where people created thousands of images in the style of Japanese animator Studio Ghibli, whose cofounder Hayao Miyazaki famously called AI-generated art “an insult to life itself.”

Anthropic has climbed to No. 2 on this year's Cloud 100 list. Anthropic has continued to be the OpenAI challenger with the most staying power. In February, it released a “hybrid reasoning” model called Claude 3.7 Sonnet that can automatically decide how to approach a question—either taking time to process it by breaking it down to smaller chunks or answering it quickly in real time. The company has also pushed into software development, releasing Claude Code, an AI system that can search and read code, edit files and run commands among a slew of other software engineering functions. CEO Dario Amodei has said that in about a year, all code might be written by AI. Most recently, Anthropic paired up with Databricks, another Cloud 100 lister, to sell AI agents—software that can autonomously carry out specific tasks—to thousands of enterprise customers. In March, Anthropic nabbed $3.5 billion in a Series E funding round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with a post-money valuation of $61.5 billion. The company released a new Claude Opus model in August, and in July, the US Department of Defense awarded Anthropic a contract of up to $200 million to work on AI capabilities that further US national security. In September, the company secured another $13 billion in a Series F funding round led by ICONIQ at a $183 billion post-money valuation.

Founded in 2009 by Irish brothers Patrick and John Collison, Stripe processes payments for online businesses. In 2024, its subscription-billing product reached more than 300,000 business customers, and it agreed to acquire Bridge, which makes infrastructure software for cryptocurrency-based stable coins (tokens that are typically pegged to the value of the U.S. dollar), for $1.1 billion. Stripe counts Nvidia, OpenAI and Pepsi among its customers.

Funding: $2.2 billion from Sequoia, General Catalyst, Founders Fund, Thrive and others.

Latest valuation: $70 billion, based on a September 2024 share purchase of $860 million by Sequoia Capital.

Date of last valuation: September 2024.

Bona fides: In the four days from Black Friday to Cyber Monday in 2024, Stripe processed more than $31 billion in transactions, up from $18.6 billion in 2023.

Cofounders: CEO Patrick Collison and president John Collison, 36 and 34, respectively, sold their first startup, an auction-management system for ecommerce sellers called Auctomatic, for $5 million in 2008 before starting Stripe.

Why IPO when you can continue raising money? That appears to be Databricks' motto. In December 2024, the data infrastructure company raised a $10 billion Series J round for a whopping $62 billion valuation–and it's currently raising a series K that may value it over $100 billion. Under the leadership of CEO Ali Ghodsi, one of seven academics from the University of California, Berkeley who cofounded the company in 2013, the startup—which has more than 15,000 customers—now plans to achieve $3.7 billion in annualized revenue by July. The company's data warehousing product, Databricks SQL, is forecast to hit $1 billion in revenue run rate by the end of the fiscal month of January 2026, and in the past year, the company—which supports AI and machine learning app development—has announced seven new offices around the globe, including offices in Mexico, Saudi Arabia and London. Databricks has also announced strategic partnerships with defense software company Palantir and generative AI company Anthropic, maker of ChatGPT competitor Claude.

Melanie Perkins—who made Forbes’ World's Richest Self-Made Women List this year—is the CEO and cofounder of Canva, a platform that sees its users whip up 376 designs every second. The $32 billion company was early to generative AI, implementing it in its popular design software, which got a revamp last May. The Australia-based company says its AI tools have been used over 18 billion times since the launch of its Magic Studio launch in 2023. Its customer roster includes T-Mobile, Salesforce, Disney and FedEx—with Canva claiming that over 95% of Fortune 500 companies use its platform. This June, the company—which laid off 10 out of 12 of its technical writers back in April, according to TechCrunch—became the first design platform to find a home in ChatGPT, embedding its creative suite into OpenAI’s personal assistant. It also integrated into Anthropic’s Claude in July and plans to integrate into Salesforce’s Agentforce in the near future.

Ramp's corporate credit card offers up to 1.5% cash back on every purchase, and its financial operations platform uses machine learning to spot wasteful spending, saving customers an average of 5% per year, the company says. Serving over 40,000 customers including CBRE, Shopify and Anduril, it expanded its offerings from a corporate card to five core product lines: corporate card and expense management, bill payments, procurement, travel and treasury. In June, Ramp raised $200 million in Series E funding at a $22.5 billion valuation. It also launched the industry's first stablecoin-backed corporate cards in partnership with Stripe and added Philadelphia Eagles star Saquon Barkley as an investor, with whom it created the company's first Super Bowl commercial in less than a week.
In July, Ramp raised another $500 million led by investment firm ICONIQ, taking its total equity financing to $1.9 billion. This allowed Ramp to reach a $22.5 billion valuation just 45 days after reaching $16 billion.

Travel and expense software company Navan offers a corporate card and an expense management app that reimburses employees' out-of-pocket business travel within 24 to 48 hours. Clients like Unilever, OpenAI, Stubhub, Adobe, Netflix and Zoom pay a subscription fee, which also allows their employees to book flights, hotels and rental cars. With over 40 offices worldwide, the company has grown through acquisitions, including Reed & Mackay, a U.K.-based travel agency, and Contravo, a German business travel platform. In 2025, it announced Navan Cognition, which helps companies create virtual agent teams that can handle a variety of tasks.

AI coding tool Cursor is among the hottest products in a very hot AI market. It’s the only product of parent company Anysphere, which is growing superfast; it’s said to have signed $100 million in contracts in about a year — a figure that has since reportedly doubled. Founded in 2022 by 24-year-old Michael Truell and three MIT classmates, Cursor helps engineers from companies including Instacart and Samsung edit code with nontechnical prompts in everyday language that can be as simple as “make me an 8-bit side-scroller video game” or “build me a weather app.” They’re already taking on giants like Github Copilot in the global market for automated coding, which is expected to reach $30 billion by 2032. “The ambition of the company is to completely change how people build software,” Truell says.

Alex Bouaziz and Shuo Wang met while in grad school at MIT, where they connected over their backgrounds as international students and children of entrepreneurs. Frustrated with trying to hire and pay their friends from other countries to work for their respective startups, they started Deel, a fully remote international payroll and compliance company which helps companies hire and pay workers from around the world. Only six years since its founding in 2019, Deel serves over 35,000 companies worldwide and boasts a $1 billion annual revenue run rate. Clients include Shopify, Coinbase, Reddit, Nike, Klarna and Hermès.

Productivity doesn’t have to be all work and no play–at least, not according to Ivan Zhao, Simon Last and Akshay Kothari, cofounders of Notion. The company created collaborative workplace software where people can brainstorm, organize and gamify their goals and work habits. Major companies like OpenAI, Figma and Toyota use the software, but it has also found popularity among Gen Z after videos of people using Notion to make weekly schedules went viral on TikTok in 2021. The influx of users from the popular app was so great that it crashed the startup’s servers. Valued at $10 billion, Notion has raised a total of $330 million from the likes of Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Index Ventures and it surpassed 100 million users last year. Aside from the free plan, Notion charges upwards of $10 per month for users to access AI features that include writing and summarizing text.

Ukraine-founded Grammarly makes the Cloud 100 list for the sixth year in a row, having appeared seven times in total. Continuing with the AI integrations for its writing assistant, the company rolled out its existing generative-AI tool–that can write, interpret and edit text–to iOS in December 2023 and Android in April 2024. The company has raised over $1.4 billion since its inception and is valued at $13 billion. Big names like Ford stand out of the 40 million people and 50,000 organizations using the company's products. In December 2024, Grammarly acquired AI productivity tool maker Coda and brought on its CEO to lead Grammarly as part of the company's push to expand its AI offerings. In July, the company also acquired Superhuman, the AI-native email app.

Alexander Rinke, Martin Klenk and Bastian Nominacher met as university students in Germany. While brainstorming on a solution for a consultancy project they were working on, they discovered research on process mining–a means of extracting meaningful data from a system's event logs–and founded Celonis in 2011 around the concept. The automation company utilizes the technique when scanning a company's existing log data, and in turn uses that to detect and visually represent its inefficiencies and bottlenecks. Based in Munich and New York, Celonis counts AstraZeneca, ASOS, Dell Technologies and Johnson & Johnson among its 1,500 customers and has raised more than $1.6 billion for a valuation of $13 billion.

Grafana Labs offers a wide range of tools allowing companies to query, visualize and understand database metrics on customizable dashboards. The company boasts a community of more than 7,000 enterprise customers, such as Nvidia, Salesforce, JPMorgan Chase and Microsoft, as well as 25 million users worldwide. Cofounders Raj Dutt, Torkel Ödegaard and Anthony Woods work on three different continents, overseeing a fully distributed startup that has raised $660 million since its formation, valuing it at $6 billion. Grafana, which started as an open source project, continues to offer open-source tools for log aggregation and data storage.

Before cofounding Netskope in 2012, Sanjay Beri scribbled an idea for a cloud security platform on a Starbucks napkin that he later pitched to Microsoft and Symantec executives. Former Symantec CEOs John Thompson and Enrique Salem both personally invested in it. Today, Netskope securely moves sensitive data in the cloud for 4,000 customers worldwide, including Elevance Health and USPTO. The company is valued at $1.4 billion and employs 3,000 workers.

When Joshua Reeves, Eddie Kim and Tomer London started Gusto in 2012, they wanted to level the playing field of payroll, benefits and other HR processes for entrepreneurs like their parents. Since then, the company has turned into a payroll powerhouse, servicing more than 400,000 small and medium-sized businesses. The company has raised more than $700 million and is valued at $9.5 billion. Recently, Gusto announced Gus, an AI-powered assistant that solves compliance challenges and automates administrative tasks. In August, the company acquired Guideline, a retirement benefit provider for small businesses valued at $1.15 billion.

Parker Conrad founded Rippling in 2016 after he was forced out of health benefits management platform provider Zenefits. After starting with human resources and IT, Rippling has expanded its offerings in an attempt to manage all aspects of employee data, from payroll and benefits to devices. Valued at $16.8 billion and having raised a total of $1.9 billion, Rippling's goal is to provide an all-in-one solution for corporate services often handled by multiple vendors.

Founded in 2007 by the father and son team of David and Orion Hindawi, Tanium was originally conceived as a “central nervous system” to secure companies against cyberthreats. Two years ago, the cofounders handed the reins over to software executive Dan Streetman. Now valued at $9 billion, the Emeryville, California-based firm has raised $1.1 billion and employs 2,000 people. Its customers include Bank of America, Best Buy and the U.S. military. Recently, Tanium announced a partnership with Microsoft to develop a new AI agent for Microsoft Security Copilot.

Miro has come a long way from its roots in Perm, Russia, where, frustrated by the challenge of showing work to clients far from the office, CEO Andrey Khusid cofounded the digital whiteboard software business in 2011 with Oleg Shardin. It has raised $475 million and is valued at $17.5 billion. Still, Miro has continued to enjoy usage momentum, claiming some 250,000 organizations including Nike, PepsiCo and Deloitte as customers. In the past two years, Miro has nearly doubled its number of users to more than 90 million. In October, Miro launched its Innovation Workspace, which it calls its most significant product launch since 2012 and combines AI assistance with enterprise-grade security.

Abnormal AI's cofounders Evan Reiser and Sanjay Jeyakumar had a background in marketing, not cybersecurity. In 2018, they started Abnormal Security with the idea of using behavioral profiling, the method that digital media companies like Twitter use to display tailored ads, to detect and block phishing email attacks. The company also uses AI to guard users from email attacks such as fake invoices and other phishing attempts. In April, the company changed its name from Abnormal Security to Abnormal AI as part of its effort to fight cybercrime with AI tools.

In 2024 alone, customers of mobile marketing platform Attentive sent more than 53 billion text messages. Attentive uses personalized messages to bring brands and consumers together for customers like Crate & Barrel, Dyson and Steve Madden. This year, Attentive released its AI Pro for Email feature to all its customers in order to help over 1,000 brands deliver more personalized messaging to inboxes.

In 2013, Cohesity founder Mohit Aron noticed data was fragmented across multiple silos and decided to build a single platform where customers could secure and manage their data. Cohesity, now valued at $9 billion, is known for its cloud data management and anti-ransomware software used by customers Nasdaq, Salesforce and Delta Airlines. Last year, the company launched Cohesity Gaia, a generative AI solution that allows customers to search, gain insights and ask questions of their own enterprise data. The company also announced a collaboration with NVIDIA–making it a new equity investor and integrating NVIDIA AI Enterprise into its Cohesity Gaia platform. Last year, Cohesity acquired Veritas' data protection unit and also exceeded $1.5 billion in annual revenue. With more than 13,600 customers, Cohesity claims to have the largest partner ecosystem in the data protection industry.

For the second year in a row, Arctic Wolf makes the top 25 on the Cloud 100 list, prompted by rising numbers of cyberattacks. Since its founding in 2012, the Eden Prairie, Minnesota-based cybersecurity company has raised close to $900 million, valuing it at $4.3 billion. Today, the company services more than 10,000 organizations ranging from small businesses to professional sports teams and government agencies. In February, Arctic Wolf acquired AI-powered threat prevention company Cylance from Blackberry.

Georgia-based Flock Safety is best known for its suite of security features used by many police departments and private users nationwide. Flock's license plate cameras have enabled it to create a database of information that includes vehicles' color, make, model and even identifiers like decals and stickers, which it sells to its law enforcement customers. The company, worth $7.5 billion, works with over 6,000 communities and more than 5,000 law enforcement agencies. Flock said that it’s helped law enforcement recover over 1,000 missing persons. This success hasn’t come without controversy: it’s currently facing scrutiny from civil liberties groups and members of Congress have recently launched an investigation into the company’s practices.

VAST Data CEO and founder Renen Hallak made an early, prescient prediction that AI models would face a growing need for data services, so he launched a company in 2016 to provide data management and infrastructure software. Since then, New York City-based VAST Data’s valuation has skyrocketed, nearly tripling from $3.7 billion in 2021 to more than $9 billion in December 2023 after a $118 million series E round. Clients like NASA, Zoom, and Pixar contribute to the $200 million in signed contracts the startup had at the end of 2023.

With a customer list that includes Microsoft and Google, AlphaSense has created a search engine that gathers insights from an extensive library of public and private sources—including earnings call transcripts, SEC filings and industry journal articles—all from one query. Its AI pieces together relevant information into a cohesive story for busy clients looking to make critical decisions fast. Led by cofounders Jack Kokko and Raj Neervannan, AlphaSense is valued at $4 billion after a $650M Series F capital raise in 2024.

Perplexity wants to make search engines without AI a thing of the past. Cofounded by Aravind Srinivas, Johnny Ho, Denis Yarats and Andy Konwinski in 2022, it uses a medley of AI models to answer users’ questions on a wide range of topics, which it backs up with footnoted sources. Srinivas, the CEO and an ex-OpenAI researcher, told Forbes last year that Perplexity is “almost like Wikipedia and ChatGPT had a kid.” It has some $900 million in total funding from the likes of Softbank and Nvidia and a $9 billion valuation, per PitchBook. In March, the CEO Srinivas claimed it had reached more than $100 million in annualized revenue. The company has drawn criticism from Forbes and other media outlets for allegedly plagiarizing their reporting and redistributing it across multiple platforms. Srinivas acknowledged that its republishing product feature had “rough edges” and that Perplexity was “improving it with more feedback.” Forbes sent a cease-and-desist letter to Perplexity in June 2024, accusing it of infringing copyright, to which the company said the claims are meritless and that factual information is not protected by copyright law.

Checkr cofounder and CEO Daniel Yanisse’s parents had to attend medical school again when they emigrated from Communist Romania to France because their degrees were not recognized in their new home. Over the 10 years since its founding, the company has committed to help unblock employment opportunities for workers by making the background check industry fairer and faster for its more than 100,000 customers, such as OpenAI, FIFA and DoorDash. The company, valued at $5 billion, offers services like an expungement solution to remove past criminal records for potential workers and a payment solution to ensure gig workers are paid accurately and on time.

Atlanta, Georgia-based OneTrust is the brainchild of Kabir Barday, who developed the idea for his company’s software while working at another company, where he saw privacy professionals struggle to comply with government regulations. Today, more than 14,000 companies use its platform, including Con Edison, World Bank and First Citizens Bank, to build privacy, trust and security programs. OneTrust has raised $1.1 billion and is valued at $4.5 billion. The company has reached $500 million in annual recurring revenue.

Founded in 2013, Plaid connects consumer bank accounts to financial apps for customers like Rocket Companies, PayPal and Citi, facilitating financial data movement across a network of more than 12,000 banks, credit unions and financial institutions. The company says it facilitates 750,000 transactions every day. This year, it launched Plaid Protect, a fraud intelligence system that it says has blocked almost 3 million instances of fraud in the past year.

Growing up in Portugal, Talkdesk CEO Tiago Paiva dreamed of someday launching his own global startup. After teaching himself to code and studying books and podcasts about U.S. entrepreneurs, he entered and won a Twilio-hosted hackathon with what would become Talkdesk. Today, companies including Accenture, AMC Networks and Patagonia use Talkdesk's cloud-based call center software, and its reach spans 100 countries. The company has raised $600 million and is valued at $10 billion.

Carta simplifies equity management for more than 7,000 funds, startups and private companies and holds $130 billion in assets under administration. The company is valued at $7.4 billion and helps over half a million equity holders use Carta in nearly 160 countries to manage cap tables, compensation and valuations. Carta has partnered with companies like Deel to automate international equity compliance, Rippling to enable startups to manage and optimize compensations and Sequoia to integrate its salary and equity data into Sequoia's Comp platform.

Postman began life as an unpaid, side-project app in Google’s Chrome Web Store to solve API challenges. But in 2014, with 500,000 users and interest from investors, CEO Abhinav Asthana teamed up with Abhijit Kane and a former colleague from his intern days at Yahoo Bangalore, Ankit Sobti, to turn Postman into a full-fledged business. Today, its 40 million users include developers at WhatsApp and PayPal, and it is the world’s leading Application Programming Interface (API) platform. The company has raised $433 million, most recently at a $5.6 billion valuation. Now, Postman has shifted into AI with features like AI-powered writing assistant Agent Mode and its AI Agent Builder.

Headquartered in Austin, Texas and Chennai, India, Zoho offers a broad suite of office software for sales and marketing, customer service and security. Bootstrapped since day one, Zoho has grown to encompass more 1 million customer organizations and 120 million users with its focus on local engagement—the company has more than 25 rural offices across the globe. In July, Zoho announced its acquisition of Asimov Robotics in a bid to further the company's push towards R&D and robotics.

After founder Howie Lui sold his company Etacts to Salesforce in 2010, he teamed up with cofounders Andrew Ofstad and Emmett Nicholas to launch Airtable three years later. Starting as a spreadsheet, calendar and to-do list combined into one, Airtable has now evolved: its prebuilt apps allow over 500,000 customer organizations such as Amazon, OpenAI and Nike to track, update and apply information across the platform. In June, Airtable rebranded itself to be AI-native, helping users find trends in their data and turn it into apps.

Dataiku offers software that lets company use their data and AI models to create new applications. The company's services are used  by more than 700 organizations worldwide, including LVMH, Morgan Stanley, Michelin, and Novartis. In 2025, Dataiku, which is valued at $3.7 billion, launched a service that gives clients the ability to build AI agents that respond to user requests.

Oakland, California-based Fivetran was founded by childhood friends George Fraser and Taylor Brown in 2012 to act as a go-between for companies that need to consolidate and transform data for better analytics. Fivetran is able to integrate data from multiple sources like Salesforce, cloud services and social media to help companies visualize data or train AI models and applications. The $5.6 billion data integration platform now has more than 7,200 global customers including Morgan Stanley, Spotify and JetBlue.

Brothers Dritan and Ledion Bitincka and CEO Clint Sharp founded Cribl in 2018 to enable IT and security companies to gather, analyze and make the most out of their data. The company, which is valued at $3.5 billion, surpassed $200 million in annual recurring revenue in January thanks to partnerships with companies like AWS, CrowdStrike and Microsoft. Last year, the company announced Cribl Copilot, an AI-powered feature that provides a chatbot, auto-generated dashboards and troubleshooting for its customers, and closed its oversubscribed $319M Series E funding round, which was led by Google Ventures.

Dialpad's CEO Craig Walker—who founded two startups that were scooped up by Google and Yahoo—grew up 10 doors down from Steve Jobs, and cites the Apple leader's design elegance and simplicity as an inspiration for his own business. Dialpad, which carried out 10 billion minutes of conversations this year, is used to provide companies like Netflix, Uber, Nasdaq and RE/MAX with customer intelligence and insights. The $2.2 billion company said it expected to reach $365 million in annual recurring revenue in August—that's $1 million in annual recurring revenue on a daily basis. Dialpad, which supports eight languages, also launched on the Google Marketplace this year.

No one likes remembering passwords, including software developers. Two couples, Dave and Sara Teare, and Roustem and Natalia Karimov, founded Toronto-based security company 1Password in 2005 to keep track of theirs. What started as a side project has since become a tool used by millions of customers and over 165,000 businesses, including IBM, Slack, Canva and Salesforce. The $6.8 billion company has raised $920 million to date. In June, the company entered into a strategic collaboration agreement with AWS to help businesses curtail security blind spots and “accelerate secure cloud adoption.”

Guillaume Pousaz, who started coding when he was eight, founded Checkout.com in 2012 to make online payment processing for shops and shoppers around the world simple. The London-based company processes billions of transactions every year for thousands of companies such as Sony, Pinterest, eBay, Klarna and Uber Eats. Supporting over 150 currencies, the $40 billion company announced plans to start issuing cards in the UAE, and in March, Intelligent Acceptance—its product that helps businesses automatically optimize payments—brought in over $10 billion in additional revenue for merchants. The company began operating in Canada this July.

Automation Anywhere was founded in 2003 by CEO Mihir Shukla, Neeti Mehta, Ankur Kothari and Rushabh Parmani. Their vision was to create software that automates repetitive business tasks like processing accounting paperwork. The $6.8 billion-company—which enables automation for 4,000 entities, including Unilever, Petrobas, and LinkedIn—has since raised $840 million in funding. In July, Automation Anywhere announced a new integration with Amazon Q Business, translating customers' natural language needs into processes executed by AI agents.

An immigrant from Pakistan who grew up in Texas, Shoaib Makani founded Motive, formerly KeepTruckin, in 2013 to connect and improve the safety of the North American trucking industry using artificial intelligence. The $2.85 billion company—which offers an AI avatar that gives drivers real-time feedback—now serves 100,000 customers in various sectors including construction, oil and gas, distribution, moving, and storage. Motive—which expects to reach $549 million in annual recurring revenue by the end of this year—acquired Carnegie Mellon’s InceptEV, an electric vehicle data company, in June. Over 1.3 million drivers use its products, which it claims have saved customers more than $3.4 million in accident, insurance and fuel costs, adding that its customers—which includes FedEx Freight, CRH Canada and CoolSys—have seen accidents reduced by up to 80%. In July, Motive secured $150 million in a private funding round that was led by Kleiner Perkins, Bloomberg reported.

Argentinian immigrant Guillermo Rauch taught himself English and software engineering at age 11 by reading software manuals. Vercel, his latest startup, allows web developers to focus on the frontend without worrying about backend servers. The company is predicated on Next.js, an open-source Web development framework Rauch authored which is actively used by over two million developers monthly at companies like Hulu, Nike and Target. Founded in 2015, the San Francisco-based company has raised $563 million, closing an Accel-led $250 million Series E funding round at a $3.25 billion valuation last year. Vercel, achieved $200M in annual recurring revenue in May with customers including Cox Enterprises, Cursor, OpenAI, Runway and Zapier. In August, the company debuted its agentic v0.app, which can “think, plan and take actions autonomously.” A previous version of that app was used by hackers to create phishing sites that looked like legit login pages, Axios reported in July. The company has since restricted access to those sites.

Think of Glean like a ChatGPT for your workplace—one that can tell you everything from how many vacation days you have left, to that obscure employee discount you'd forgotten. The AI-powered search tool—used by over 1 million employees on teams at companies like Booking.com, Deutsche Telekom and Duolingo—is trained on a company's entire database, allowing employees to get quick access to their pressing questions by pinging customizable AI agents in Slack, Teams and Zendesk. In February, the unicorn company claimed it had $100 million in annualized revenue, and in June, the company secured $150 million in a Series F funding round led by Wellington Management—upping its valuation to $7.2 billion. Glean Agents, which the company introduced in May, allows employees to create and scale agents without coding.

Airwallex CEO Jack Zhang launched a café in Melbourne in 2015, and one of the challenges he faced in that business was the cost and complexity of sending payments to suppliers overseas. He founded Airwallex in 2015 to serve as an international payments and finance platform with features like multi-currency accounts, borderless cards, expense management and online payments. Over 150,000 businesses around the globe now use this platform, including TikTok, Qantas, SHEIN, Rippling and Navan. Airwallex has achieved $900 million in annualized revenue as of July, growing 89% year over year compared to last June. The Australia-founded company recently raised $300 million in a Series F funding round from Square Peg, DST Global, Salesforce Ventures, Visa Ventures and others—bringing its valuation to $6.2 billion. In July, Airwallex secured a license which allows the company to offer its solutions to businesses in Israel. That same month, Airwallex also became the official finance software partner of pro soccer club Arsenal, giving the team a way to receive payments around the world via multiple currencies.

The Vancouver-based company develops legal tools software that enables law firms to automate processes such as client intake, accounting and document management. The company also has a generative AI solution that helps lawyers complete routine tasks and audit logs for court discovery. Over 200,000 legal experts use Clio, whose software is endorsed by more than 100 law societies and bar associations around the globe, including all 50 state bar associations in the United States. Clio, which has raised a total of $1.29 billion to date, announced in June it would acquire vLex—the company behind Vincent AI, an AI-powered legal research assistant—for $1 billion.

NinjaOne debuts in this year's Cloud 100 list at 47. The company’s founders—CEO Sal Sferlazza and Chris Matarese—met at summer camp at the age of six and went on to start multiple companies together when they grew up. Sferlazza felt that IT software on the market was complex and that it lacked support and product focus, so in 2013, the duo founded NinjaOne, which aims to bring simplicity to IT and security spaces via its platform. Twelve years later, NinjaOne now boasts 30,000-plus customers including Nvidia, Nissan, Lyft and PGA Tour. In February, NinjaOne secured $500 million in funding, bringing its total amount raised to $761.5 million. In June, the $5 billion valuation company acquired Dropsuite—a cloud backup platform—for approximately $270 million and announced its availability on the Google Cloud Marketplace in July.

Every month, Zapier users automate over 3.1 billion tasks across 8,000-plus apps. The remote-first company, which was launched out of a Missouri hackathon in 2011, has been largely self-sustaining—raising only $1.4 million in outside funding with a $5 billion valuation.  Last year, it acquired the team behind AI-powered video conferencing tool Vowel, and this year, Zapier launched its Model Context Protocol server, which allows users to link their AI assistants, such as Claude, to over 7,000 apps without elaborate API integrations. Zapier counts Canva, Webflow, Miro and other Cloud 100 companies among its 3.4 million customers.

Twin brothers Michael and Stephen Balaban founded Lambda as an AI photo editing app in 2012, but saw a bigger opportunity when their app ran up tens of thousands of dollars in compute bills from cloud provider Amazon Web Services. In 2017, they began building their own cluster of graphic processing units (GPUs) to sell to other companies. Since then, demand for the San Jose, California-based company's hardware and cloud computing services has skyrocketed with the AI boom. The unicorn— valued at $2.5 billion—has become a top GPU cloud for developers at organizations like Intel, Microsoft and the Department of Defense, allowing them to build, test and deploy AI products at scale. Lambda boasts 15,000 paying customers and has raised over $863 million in investment to date, most recently a $480 million Series D co-led by Andra Capital and SGW in February 2025.

Founded in 2016 by Pedro Franceschi and Henrique Dubugras, Brex provides corporate credit cards, business accounts, expense management software and other financial services, particularly for high-growth, venture-backed companies whose spending appears outsized compared with cash flow. Companies like Doordash, Five Guys, SeatGeek and Robinhood are some of the 250 public companies using Brex to increase their efficiency by tracking all company spend in one place, in real time with more than 30,000 customers using Brex overall. In May, Brex partnered with procurement orchestration platform Zip to launch Brex for Zip, which gives employees—such as those at Anthropic, Coinbase and Neuralink—access to virtual cards within Zip which they can use for purchase orders, invoice payments and more.  In August, Brex obtained a license to conduct operations in the European Union.

Snyk's founder, Guy Podjarny, brought on board member Peter McKay as CEO in 2019 with the goal of making Snyk's developer security tools available to around 30 million global developers. The Boston-based company counts Spotify, Kroger, CVS Health and Salesforce among its over 4,500 customers. The company recently exceeded $300 million in annual recurring revenue with its AI code checker, Snyk Code, bringing in $100 million alone. In May, the company launched its AI Trust Platform, which helps teams reduce risk and keep AI applications secure. Snyk has racked up two acquisitions this year, Invariant Labs—a security research lab—and Probley—a vulnerability scanner, raising its total acquisition count to 12.

Before Gong, cofounder Amit Bendov was CEO at business software company SiSense. After a “quarter from hell” in which his sales pipeline shrunk without warning and tanked revenues, Bendov came up with the idea for an AI-powered product that monitors sales decisions. Gong, which he founded in 2015 with Eilon Reshef, automatically records sales calls, transcribes them and analyzes their contents. Gong has since grown into a business valued at $7.25 billion, with more than 4,700 companies now using the platform, including Google, Reddit, Dolby and ADP. Last year, Gong launched Ask Anything, a generative AI-powered query solution across calls and emails that has been trained on more than 3 billion customer interactions. In March, the company—which opened offices in New York and Austin this August—announced over $300 million in annual recurring revenue. In May, Gong joined forces with Microsoft to integrate its platform into Microsoft 365 Copilot, Teams and Outlook.

Intercom was conceived at a cafe in Dublin, Ireland by Eoghan McCabe, Des Traynor, Ciaran Lee and David Barrett. The $1.3 billion company started out by building messaging tools for businesses to communicate with its now 25,000-plus customers, and it first crossed $100 million in revenue under CEO McCabe. But he stepped down in 2020, a year after reports that he made unwanted advances toward junior female employees. In October of 2022, McCabe returned as CEO, telling Forbes he had been cleared by inside and outside investigations. Since then, McCabe has bet big on AI: the company rolled out its AI agent Fin in March 2023, launched an AI lab in Dublin last February and announced an approximately $100 million investment to develop Fin last May. Used by Anthropic, Solidcore, Shutterstock and Pfizer, Fin—which saw capabilities like Fin Voice and Fin Insights roll out this year—is expected to surpass $100 million in annual recurring revenue next year.

Guild was cofounded in 2015 by Rachel Romer, a former Obama administration official, as a research initiative in the community college sector to improve education for adult learners. Last year, longtime exec Bijal Shah took over as CEO, and today, the company offers over 2,000 programs for workers to upskill and grow in their careers–all at their employer's expense. Partnering with customers like Chipotle, Discover, Hilton and Target, the Colorado-based company provides learning programs, career development and one-on-one coaching for their staff. This year, Guild—valued at $4.40 billion per PitchBook—partnered with Walgreens to launch PharmStart, which helps Walgreens employees meet the pre-reqs for pharmacy school, and partnered with Din Tai Fung to launch ElevateU, which gives employees access to an English language learning program.

Ronni Zehavi and Israel David cofounded HR platform HiBob in 2015 to be what Zehavi calls the “Instagram of HR tech.” The London and Tel Aviv-based startup sells HR software that helps with tasks like onboarding, payroll and performance management via a friendly, accessible interface called “Bob.” Used by the likes of VaynerMedia, Zenoti and Fiverr, the company has over 4,500 customers around the globe. In September 2023, it closed a $150 million funding round, boosting its valuation to $2.7 billion. Last year, HiBob acquired UK-based payroll automation system Pento for $40 million and in February 2025 it acquired Mosaic, a financial planning and analysis platform. The company—with 1.1 million users and over 1,300 employees across seven global offices—went from $10 million in annual recurring revenue in 2020 to $197 million in 2025.

CEO Felix Van de Maele was a 23-year-old graduate student studying how machines understand data at the University of Brussels when the 2008 financial crisis hit. He saw an opportunity to use his research to help banks deal with new compliance standards. Today, his cloud-based data governance platform helps data professionals with moving, storing, transforming and analyzing data while managing its governance and compliance.  Last year, the $5.3 billion company launched AI Governance, an AI tool to help customers like IKEA, Toyota and SAP deliver quality data to AI models and maintain regulatory compliance, and in June, Collibra acquired data access governance platform Raito as well as metadata solution platform Deasy Labs.

Practicing cardiologist Dr. Shiv Rao founded Abridge in 2018 to free clinicians from the time-sucking paperwork that's required after they see patients: jotting down detailed notes for their medical records. Instead, Abridge records their conversations with patients and uses AI to both summarize them and fill out electronic health forms. Thousands of clinicians at health systems like John Hopkins Medicine and Mayo Clinic are already using it. In June, the startup announced a $300 million series E funding round supported by Andreessen Horowitz and Khosla Ventures, bumping its valuation to $5.3 billion.

Oren Kaniel didn't have a background in marketing or traditional technology when he cofounded AppsFlyer in San Francisco in 2011, but since then the company has become a leader in the analytics market, working with over 100,000 apps from 15,000 brands. The $2 billion company provides advanced measurement, data analytics and marketing metrics to customers like CNN, Louis Vuitton, State Farm and Whataburger. In February, the company—which has a 60% market share—laid off approximately 100 employees, citing a desire for increased “investments in AI” and the prioritization of “high-value initiatives.” In July, Appsflyer launched a Model Context Protocol that links its APIs to large language models. The tool, built on Anthropic’s MCP framework, is currently available via Claude.

Finding back and forth emails for meeting scheduling inefficient, Tope Awotona quit his job and poured his life savings into his automated scheduling platform, Calendly, which he founded in 2013. Today, the Nigerian-born entrepreneur is the CEO of a $3 billion business and a billionaire. Calendly makes it easy for customers or clients to set up appointments by displaying someone's availability and allowing them to choose a time and date that works. More than 20 million users and 100,000 organizations across 230-plus countries employ Calendly's appointment scheduler. In March, Calendly rolled out an integration into LinkedIn that allows LinkedIn Premium Business users to display a button on their profiles to book meetings.

If a pharma company wants to understand the market for its next drug, or an insurance provider wants to assess which patients might be at higher risk for illness, they increasingly turn to Komodo Health. The over $3 billion company offers an anonymized database of 330 million patients' hospital visits and an analytics platform to put that data to work. Named for the Komodo dragon, the company launched life sciences platform MapLab in September 2023 and analytics application MapView in March 2024. In May, Komodo partnered with Nasdaq, giving venture capital firms a way to monitor trends in the pharmaceutical and healthcare spaces. In June, Komodo launched MapLab Enterprise, its AI-native healthcare analytics platform for organizations seeking to bring consistency to their data foundation.

Workato was cofounded in 2013 by Vijay Tella with the intention of automating workflows through its no-code platform. Tella is an immigrant from rural India, who became inspired to run a company after observing his father's work as a mining executive. The company—valued at $5.7 billion has 12,000 customers across the globe at companies like H&M, Toyota Motor Europe and Hubspot. Having automated over 750 billion actions this year, Workato—which moved up slightly from last year’s ranking—has been active in the agentic space with its Workato ONE launch in March, its Workato GO launch in June and the launch of three AgentX Apps in AWS Marketplace in July.

If you've ever made a restaurant reservation through OpenTable or logged a sale in Salesforce, your interaction with the app may have been logged in the cloud by Pendo. The Raleigh, North Carolina-based company helps customers capture user behavior and feedback for review so they can prioritize the development of updates and features that will most improve the user experience. The $2.6 billion company—whose 14,400-plus customers include United Airlines, Cisco and Morgan Stanley—acquired Israel-based predictive analytics platform Forwrd this July, whose tech now serves as the underpinning for Pendo Predict, which rolls out in October. Pendo Predict promises to make intelligent suggestions, helping teams find ways to increase revenue and propel retention. In July, Pendo announced the opening of a data center in Australia.

For enterprises, data security and compliance can be a gnarly process, often prone to errors. Vanta wants to help companies stay honest about how they handle their customers’ data. Its solution: continuous monitoring tools and automated security reports that provide a clear picture of where vulnerabilities lie. Over 12,000 customers including Atlassian, Omni Hotels, Duolingo and Snowflake now use its software to automate their security compliance processes. Founded by Stanford graduate Christina Cacioppo—one of America’s richest self-made women—and backed by VCs like Sequoia and CrowdStrike Ventures, the unicorn closed a Series D funding round in July, boosting its total funding to $504 million and its valuation to $4.15 billion. That same month, Vanta announced its acquisition of Riskey—which offers real-time risk monitoring solutions—and in June, the company debuted its Vanta AI Agent to support governance, risk and compliance teams. In August, the company announced a partnership with XBOW which gives teams access to autonomous AI-powered pen testing via Vanta's platform.

With a vision of helping people without coding skills build websites, cofounder Vlad Magdalin—who left the USSR as a refugee when he was nine—took on nearly $30,000 in credit card debt in 2013 to launch Webflow with his brother Sergie and Bryant Chou. Capitalizing on fast-growing interest in so-called “no code” software for non-technical users, the venture—which Magdalin initially struggled to build over nearly 10 years —finally took off. Last year, former president and COO Linda Tong took the helm as CEO. Now Webflow, which has 3.5 million total users, is valued at $4 billion and has 300,000 paid customers, including Discord, Dropbox, Spotify and Orangetheory Fitness. In July, the company supported Cloudflare in its launch of permission-based controls for website owners, allowing them, by default, to prohibit AI crawlers from crawling their sites without permission.

As Israelis working in the U.S., Forter cofounders Michael Reitblat and Liron Damri were frustrated when their online credit card transactions were sometimes declined for no apparent reason. They soon realized that online payments were often flagged for overly broad reasons like an address in a country with a high number of fraudulent transactions. Using their background in Israeli military intelligence, Reitblat and Damri built Forter, an accurate fraud detection system for e-commerce that comes into contact with 1.8 billion shoppers. Since inception, Forter, which is valued at $3 billion, according to PitchBook, has processed over $2 trillion worth of ecommerce transactions for customers including Adobe, Nordstrom, Instacart and Chick-fil-A. In April, Forter launched a beta test version of its Predictive Payment Routing, which utilizes AI to find the most optimal payment route for transactions.

At the age of 22, Sajith Wickramasekara dropped out of MIT. His business venture that followed is now valued at $6.1 billion. CEO Wickramasekara and Ashu Singhal founded Benchling with scientists—those making groundbreaking discoveries in disciplines such as gene editing and protein folding—in mind. The cloud-based platform is used by researchers across more than 1,300 biotech companies and 7,500 academic labs to record and organize scientific data. Its customers are found across more than 32 countries and include pioneering biotech and biopharma companies Moderna, Sanofi and Merck, which use the platform for research and development, with thousands of academic labs around the globe using the platform at no cost. Last May, the company announced $200 million in annualized revenue, and this year, Benchling launched Benchling Assistants, which saves scientists time by automating lab work,  as well as Deep Research—an search engine that uses experimental data and literature to answer user questions. In January, Benchling laid off 10 percent of its staff, according to Endpoints News.

BrowserStack was founded by Ritesh Arora and Nakul Aggarwal in 2011 while they were roommates at India’s IIT Bombay.  Today, Browerstack is a software testing platform powering over two million tests every day by more than two million developers. BrowserStack helps Google, Twitter, Microsoft and 50,000 other customers deliver quality software at speed by moving testing to their cloud. The $4 billion company has expanded its product portfolio to become an end-to-end test platform that allows complete development of applications from inception to finish. Browserstack announced a partnership with Microsoft to support users transitioning to BrowserStack’s device testing platform, ensuring a seamless migration for developers.

Describe it, design it. That's how people are using Midjourney's popular AI image generation tool, which is available via Discord and web app. CEO David Holz—a former NASA researcher who previously founded Leap Motion—started the San Francisco-based business in 2021. It has since been used to create everything from floral typography and watercolor-style art to realistic-looking images of Pope Francis or U.S. President Donald Trump, tapping into video generation with the release of its V1 Video Model in June. Midjourney—which brought in $300 million in total revenue in the 2024 fiscal year, according to PitchBook—has so far shunned any outside funding, but it did announce a technology licensing partnership with Meta in August. Midjourney was also hit with a lawsuit this June, with Disney and Universal suing for copyright infringement. In August, Midjourney pushed back and argued fair use for AI model training, writing that “Copyright law does not confer absolute control over the use of copyrighted works.”

Munich-based Personio provides all-in-one HR software to over 15,000 small and medium-sized European companies, simplifying workplace planning and payroll. It raised $200 million in 2022 at an $8.5 billion valuation to help it prepare for rocky markets, bringing its total funding to $720 million. In April, the company celebrated its tenth birthday by relaunching its website with new metrics features. Despite laying off 115 employees late last year, it has continued to expand offerings, including an Employer of Record service aimed at streamlining international hiring in partnership with HR provider Remote.

San Diego, California-based ClickUp was originally conceived by founder Zeb Evans as an internal tool to manage his team’s work in one place. Today, Evans helms a $4 billion company with over 14 million users that boasts customers like Nike, Google and Netflix. The all-in-one tool offers services for workers to collaborate on documents, manage projects, track timelines and get insights from analytics dashboards. ClickUp’s latest releases include a revamped calendar with integrated AI notetaking, a new chat feature, and Brain MAX — an app that consolidates control over different AI tools so they can be used at once instead of switching between them. In May, the company acquired Bulgarian project management startup Ora.pm and Norwegian startup Kitemaker.

Automattic is the company behind popular blogging service WordPress. Founded in 2005 by then-aspiring web developer Matt Mullenweg, it has grown into a global company valued at $7.5 billion as of its latest October 2021 financing. The company's open-source CMS is used by  customers like Samsung, CNN, and Chevron, and its e-commerce service powers over 1.4 million shops online. Automattic's family of products includes WordPress.com, WooCommerce and Jetpack. The company recently acquired relationship management startup Clay while boosting its investments in digital publishing by acquiring Harper and WPAI. It also launched an AI website builder and added new pay-to-use features for redesigned chat app Beeper.

ClickHouse creator Alexey Milovidov cofounded the Portola Valley, California-based company in 2021 with ex-Salesforce exec Aaron Katz and ex-Netflix exec Yury Izrailevsky. Since then, its database of real-time analytics and data warehousing has been used by leading AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as tech stalwarts like Cisco and Sony. ClickHouse acquired observability platform HyperDX in March. Two months later, it raised $350M in a Series C funding round led by Khosla Ventures, tripling its valuation to $6.4 billion. Most recently, enterprise sales veteran Kevin Egan, who was previously at Atlassian, Slack and Dropbox, joined the company as its Chief Revenue Officer.

The cofounders of New York City-based Axonius met while serving in an intelligence unit of the Israeli military. The startup helps enterprises' IT and security teams manage software applications, users and devices. Axonius is projected to cross $200 million in annual recurring revenue in 2025 and now has over 670 customers, including Anheuser-Busch, Lending Tree and City of Los Angeles. The company also operates a subsidiary organization that supports four of the five major U.S. Department of Defense service agencies. In April, it launched a suite of cyber asset management products that have been implemented by customers like Texas A&M University to improve security.

Algolia’s culture-first leadership has led the search engine company to over 18,000 users and customers in more than 130 countries. It began as a search engine tailored for mobile apps but quickly pivoted to a broader vision, offering search-as-a-service. Companies feed their data through its software, and Algolia provides letter-by-letter search results to visitors, so they feel like they're searching Google or their own files. The $2.3 billion company runs 2 trillion searches every year and serves customers like PetSmart and Walgreens. In June, it expanded offerings to provide AI agents with real-time business context.

One of Google Translate's top rivals, DeepL was founded in 2017 by Polish entrepreneur Jaroslaw Kutylowski. Its AI-powered software enables users to translate text and files into 30 different languages, including Estonian, Japanese and Portuguese, or to make writing in another language sound more natural. DeepL's free basic service has been used by millions of people, and it claims to have more than 200,000 business users, including Zendesk, Coursera and Klarna. In May 2024, the Cologne, Germany-based company cracked a $2 billion valuation. It achieved HIPAA compliance earlier this year, which enables its translation services to be integrated into healthcare tools. In March, the company launched Clarify, an interactive feature to help users understand translation decisions.

What started as an AI chatbot for teens in 2016 has become an open-source platform worth $4.5 billion. Founded by Clement Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf, Hugging Face has some 10 million users who use it to share code and collaborate on models, datasets and apps. The platform hosts a library of models and datasets from 215,000 firms including Meta and Microsoft as well as government organizations like France's Ministry of Culture, Poland's Ministry of Digital Affairs and UNESCO. The company has raised a total of $395.2 million in funding from tech heavyweights like Amazon, Google and Nvidia. It acquired Pollen Robotics in April and launched its first-ever robotics product, Reachy Mini, which gathered over $1 million in sales in less than a week.

Harness CEO and cofounder Jyoti Bansal has been here before. He led his previous company AppDynamics to No. 9 on the inaugural Cloud 100 list in 2016 and was hours away from taking it public the following year before Cisco swooped in to acquire it at a $3.7 billion price tag. Through its “startup within a startup” model, Bansal's next venture Harness encourages his employees to pitch him different ideas and products. The result is software that helps developers to build and ship applications more efficiently. It is projected to cross $250 million in annual recurring revenue in 2025 and merged with another of his companies — API security startup Traceable — in February. United Airlines, HP and Lloyds Bank are among the San Francisco-based firm’s over 600 customers.

Island cofounders Mike Fey and Dan Amiga met in 2017 when enterprise cloud company Symantec, where Fey was president and COO, acquired Amiga’s cybersecurity startup Fireglass for $250 million. Amiga had a hunch that open-source project Chromium could solve the inherent challenges with his web security technology and tapped Fey to lead the pair’s new startup after he left Symantec in 2018. The hunch has paid off–in March, Island raised over $730 million in total funding, including a $250M Series E that pushed its valuation to nearly $5 billion. It added Citi Ventures, J.P. Morgan Growth Equity Partners, and ServiceNow Ventures as strategic investors.

Equipment maintenance startup MaintainX grew from a tool cobbled together from Google Docs and Slack to a $2.5 billion venture when cofounders Chris Turlica and Hugo Dozois-Caouette found that existing computerized maintenance management systems were clunky, expensive and inaccessible to technicians on the field. Serving over 11,000 companies worldwide, its customer portfolio includes Hunter Douglas, Cintas, and Duracell, with the company managing over 11 million assets across manufacturing, facilities management, food and beverage and more. In July, it raised $150M in Series D funding, backed by a slew of investors including Bessemer Venture Partners, Bain Capital Ventures and Hashicorp CEO Dave McJannet.

Changing the sound of your voice, cloning your voice, or even making yourself sound like you're speaking in a different language is all possible with ElevenLabs' software. The generative AI audio company has 45 pre-made voices for dubbing podcasts, narrating audiobooks and creating voiceovers. CEO Mati Staniszewski started the company with childhood friend Piotr Dabkowski in 2022 after being frustrated by poorly dubbed films. The Polish duo landed on the Forbes 30 Under 30 Europe list last year and have raised $281 million for their company at a valuation of $3.3 billion. But it has also taken heat from voice actors, who have sued the company for allegedly cloning their voices without permission (ElevenLabs has asked for the claims to be dismissed due to a lack of evidence). The software was also used to create a fake robocall that imitated Biden's voice, urging voters in New Hampshire not to vote. In response, ElevenLabs reportedly suspended the account behind the deepfake for violating its policies. In August, the company launched Eleven Music, which uses text prompts to generate songs and is available for commercial use.

Shlomo Kramer's first two cybersecurity ventures — Check Point and Imperva — respectively pioneered the first commercial and web application firewalls. Founded on their heels in 2015, Tel Aviv-based Cato Networks enables its 3,500-plus customers, such as Carlsberg Group, Ulta Beauty and Hafele, to connect to resources from anywhere around the world. The company surpassed $250 million in annual recurring revenue in 2024. In June, it announced a $359 million Series G funding round that pushed its valuation to over $4.8 billion. An extension in September, brought total funding to $409 million and pushed Cato's valuation to $5.2 billion.

Cofounders Yotam Segev and Tamar Bar-Ilan, CEO and CTO of Cyera, built and ran the cloud security division for the Israeli Defense Force's elite Unit 8200. Now, their venture is said to be the world's fastest-growing AI-native data security company. Across two rounds of funding over eight months, Cyera – which splits headquarters between New York and Tel Aviv – doubled its valuation to $6 billion. Its recent $540M Series E funding was led by Georgian, Greenoaks, and Lightspeed Venture Partners and valued the company at $6 billion. The company has expanded to 10 countries, doubled in size to 800 employees, and onboarded Dave Rogers, previously of Palo Alto Networks, to expand its partnerships. Sol Rashidi, who helped launch IBM Watson, also recently joined the company as its Chief Strategy Officer for Data and AI.

Lights, camera, Runway. Imagine cutting your video editing time from five hours to five minutes. That's exactly what the graphics team at The Late Show with Stephen Colbert has done with Runway—a startup valued $3.3 billion. Founded by Cristóbal Valenzuela, Anastasis Germanidis and Alejandro Matamala in 2018, Runway's AI image and video tools allow users to conjure up images and videos on the fly—from location changes and lighting adjustments to recasts of a character. Visual effects artist Evan Halleck used Runway to assist with the rock scene in the Oscar-winning film Everything Everywhere All at Once. This year, the New York City-based startup raised $308M in Series D funding and announced partnerships with Lionsgate, AMC Networks and Netflix.

Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao is one of the pioneers of what's called “compound AI” systems—techniques that use multiple AI models that each tackle specific tasks, rather than one larger model that tries to do it all. Her company, Fireworks AI, a Forbes Next Billion-Dollar Startup listmaker, provides the background infrastructure for AI developers to run more than 100 generative AI models and decide which one is the best for a given application. It boasts customers like Samsung, Doordash and Verizon, and has caught the eye of investors like Sequoia Capital and Nvidia. Last July, it raised a $52 million funding round at a valuation of $552 million.

Belgium-based business management company Odoo was founded in 2005 by CEO Fabien Pinckaers, who featured on the 2025 Forbes Billionaires list. Pinckaers created Odoo at 22, as a software project to manage the flow of beer kegs in a student party room on campus. The company recently partnered with Wishket to help small and medium-sized Korean enterprises move more of their operations into digital. The company rose to a $5.3 billion valuation after raising $527M in secondary investment led by CapitalG and Sequoia Capital.

San Francisco-based Together AI provides cloud computing services and software to 700,000 AI developers and enterprises like Zoom, Salesforce and Quora to train, fine tune and run AI models. The company is also a staunch advocate for open-source AI technology and hosts 200 open source models for video, image and text generation. Since its founding in 2022, it's become one of the largest resources for open source data to train large language models, thanks to its dataset named RedPajama-V2 that contains more than 30 trillion units of data. Earlier this year, the company reached a valuation of $3.3 billion after closing a $305 million round led by General Catalyst, and acquired Refuel.ai in May.

“Dbt” stands for data build tool, which, aptly, is the name of Dbt Labs’ flagship product. The company is known for its free-to-use, open source data analytics tool and aims to lower the technical barrier to transforming raw data into analysis-ready models. It is currently used by the likes of Siemens, Roche and Condé Nast, and early this year crossed two milestones —  reaching more than 5,000 customers and hitting $100 million in annual recurring revenue. After the company announced a new integration with Salesforce last year, it acquired SDF Labs and launched its dbt Fusion engine in May, improving the speed and scale of its operations.

Turkish-American engineers Burkay Gur and Gorkem Yurtseven cofounded Fal.ai as a solution to the infrastructure bottlenecks they ran into while working at Coinbase and Amazon. Its software is used by over 1 million developers as well as customers like Adobe, Canva and Perplexity. The company powers generative content creation through AI-audio, video and images, and in February, it raised $49M in Series B funding led by Notable Capital. It has projected its annual recurring revenue to grow by 300 percent by the end of the year.

If this $2 billion (valuation) startup has its way, your next job interview might be conducted by a robot. Mercor uses AI to automate the employment application process, identifying standout candidates from reams of cover letters and résumés and screening them via video calls with avatars. The idea is to make hiring less subjective, instead of the “very vibes-based assessment” of traditional interviews, says CEO Brendan Foody. “Our models are able to figure out the features on résumés that are actually predictive.” Foody and his cofounders, all age 21, dropped out of college to start Mercor. They're all Thiel Fellows, recipients of the $100,000 grants billionaire Peter Thiel gives to young entrepreneurs willing to skip school.

The brainchild of college classmates Edith Harbaugh and John Kodumal, LaunchDarkly has raised $330 million in total funding, most recently in August 2021 at a $3 billion valuation. Over 5,500 customers like Autodesk, Paramount Studios and Christian Dior use its feature management service, which enables developers to launch code and features gradually to a subset of users, thus avoiding crashes and bugs that could affect their entire customer base. At its Galaxy conference in May, the company announced the launch of AI Configs, used to customize and test large language models within AI applications. It also acquired application monitoring platform Highlight.io and Houseware, a frontrunner in warehouse-native product analytics.

Lawyers' desks are notoriously covered in paperwork, but Harvey can make all that clutter disappear. The AI company is built to securely store thousands of sensitive documents – including court records – and quickly allow lawyers to get answers to complex legal queries. Winston Weinberg and Gabriel Pereyra cofounded the startup in 2022, and in the past year it has grown from 40 customers to 235, including the majority of top 10 U.S. law firms. Recently, the startup raised a $300 million series E round, boosting its valuation to $5 billion, and announced plans to expand coverage to India, Australia and Germany.

Sierra is the latest act for its CEO Bret Taylor, the OpenAI board member who was formerly Facebook CTO, Salesforce co-CEO and Twitter chairman. He started the company in 2023 with longtime Google veteran Clay Bavor with the belief that ChatGPT-style conversational AI agents would transform the way businesses interact with their customers. Those include text chats as well as voice agents, who can talk people through flight changes, shopping returns or banking questions. Traction from customers including Sonos and The North Face has helped Taylor and Bavor to raise $285 million from top VC firms Benchmark and Sequoia, reaching a $4.5 billion valuation last fall. In September, the company announced they've raised another $350 million at a valuation of $10 billion, led by Greenoaks.

Papaya Global's automated global payroll and human resources software is utilized by more than 1,000 companies in over 160 countries. Under cofounder Eynat Guez, the first female CEO to lead a unicorn tech startup in Israel, the company has been outspoken on social change. Its employee base has a nearly 50-50 male-female ratio and the company describes itself as the “moral compass of the tech sector in Israel.” In July, the company launched Papaya Payments Academy — an on-demand training site for workplace payments — and announced partnerships with Citi and Worksome.

In 2016, Cloud 100 newcomer Brightwheel got an early boost from “Shark Tank,” where investors Mark Cuban and Chris Sacca wrote founder and CEO Dave Vasen a check for $600,000. Its early-education software for preschools and daycares lets teachers share tens of millions of photos, videos and learning activities with parents each month. In July, the company released a roadmap of upcoming features, including form improvements, tuition and fee agreements, and an updated curriculum. Brightwheel has raised a total of $158 million in investment backing and is valued at $735 million.

When freelancing in the beauty industry, GlossGenius cofounder Danielle Cohen-Shohet saw that scheduling, payments, and other back-office work swallowed more hours than the work itself. That inspired Danielle and her identical twin sister Leah to build a digital-receipt point-of-sale app to give salons and small businesses a competitive edge in payments and client management. The company now serves over 96,000 local beauty and wellness businesses, from single owner operators to high-profile celebrity spots like Cynthia Erivo’s nail salon and A$AP Rocky’s hair stylist. It reportedly powers over 1 million appointments per week and crossed $100 million in annual recurring revenue over the past year.

Entrepreneurs Galina Antova and Amir Zilberstein and cybersecurity researcher Benny Porat started Claroty in 2015 with the mission of protecting critical physical infrastructure. Since then, the cyber defense company has raised over $700 million in investment and boasts $300 million in annual recurring revenue over the past three years. Claroty’s research team — Team 82 — made over 650 CPS vulnerability discoveries, the most of any research team in the sector. The company has signed a multi-year Strategic Collaboration Agreement with Amazon Web Services and serves over 1,000 customers worldwide, including Pfizer, General Motors, Siemens and Coca-Cola.

Chainguard’s founding team, who first worked together at Google, built the $3.5 billion security startup in the aftermath of the SolarWinds attack. That extensive,  high-level breach compromised thousands of organizations– including U.S. government agencies– and prompted CEO Dan Lorenc and his team to consider how such attacks could be prevented. Since then, Chainguard helps organizations like Snowflake and Finfare safeguard against the fragility of the software supply chain. Earlier this year, the company announced partnerships with Datadog, Azul and Raft. In April, it raised $356M in a Series D funding round co-led by Kleiner Perkins and IVP.

To create videos in 140 languages, simply write a script, pick from one of 230 synthetic avatars and voila! Instavideo. Founded in 2017 by a team of academics and entrepreneurs, Synthesia's generative AI tools are used to create corporate marketing materials as well as influencers' TikTok videos. Big outfits like Reuters and Accenture are among its 65,000 clients. In January, Synthesia landed an additional $180 million in funding and nabbed a $2 billion valuation. CEO Victor Riparbelli—an alumnus of the Forbes 30 Under 30 list—says Synthesia's tech still has room to grow and its avatars could become more realistic. Most recently, Synthesia crossed $100 million in annual recurring revenue and received investment backing from Adobe Ventures for an undisclosed amount.

Kareem Amin has a unique background for a tech founder: He once worked in journalism. Before starting Clay, a $3.1 billion unicorn that makes AI-powered spreadsheets for sales teams, he was the vice president of product for the Wall Street Journal, where he developed software that let reporters publish data-driven articles on mobile phones. “I was really interested in building tools for programming for non-programmers,” Amin says. “In that case, it was journalists.” Now the target is businesses both large and small. Corporate clients OpenAI and Anthropic use Clay to organize sales leads and suss out new ones. A protein-shake vendor, say, could use its software to pull location, phone numbers and user ratings on gyms across the country.

After cofounder Ray Mieszaniec’s father was permanently disabled in a car accident, systemic inequities in personal injury law led to his claim being settled for less money than his losses. Determined to bring change, Ray joined CEO Rami Karabibar and CPO Saam Mashhad to build EvenUp. The $1 billion company now powers over 1,500 personal injury firms, helping to analyze medical records and generating over $7 billion in claims to date. Its expansion efforts include new headquarters in San Francisco and the launch of workflow tools to reduce delays in document draft and review times. Last year, the company also raised $135M in Series D funding led by Bain Capital Ventures.
